1. Keeping Your API Key Private
The .env file should NOT be included if you plan to share your program publicly or upload it somewhere like GitHub.

Your .env file is meant to be local and private, containing your personal API key only.

You can add .env to a .gitignore file to prevent accidental upload to GitHub.

When sharing your program (e.g., the .exe), do NOT include your .env file.

2. What about the .exe file?
PyInstaller bundles your Python code inside the .exe.

If you hard-code your API key in the source, it will be inside the .exe and could be extracted by someone skilled.

But if your program loads the API key only from .env at runtime, the .exe itself doesn't have your API key inside.

So, sharing the .exe without your .env file means other users can run it by providing their own API key.

3. Best practice
Distribute your .exe without the .env file.

Make the program prompt users to enter their own API key on first run and save it locally in .env on their machine.

Never share your .env file publicly.

Use .gitignore for .env when using GitHub.

4. About antivirus vendors like Norton
If you submit your program for scanning without your API key, they only see the executable and code — no API key.

If you send the .env with your API key, they will see it. So don’t do that.

Bottom line: Keep your .env private, do not include it in shares or repos, and make the app request the API key on first use.

If you want, I can help adjust the code so it always prompts for the API key if .env is missing! Would you like that?
